input.summary: I ran the checks the request asks for against the current application and left the filing text untouched, because nothing in it is defective. Both mechanical failures have a single cause: the sheets for FIG. 3, FIG. 4, FIG. 5 and FIG. 6 have not been rendered. All six brief files are present in figures/ and each is complete, so the drawing plan itself is sound. I verified numeral coverage sheet by sheet: FIG. 1 carries 100, 10, 12, 14, 16, 30, 40 and 90; FIG. 2 carries 20, 22, 24, 26, 28 and 34; FIG. 3 carries 18, 20, 30, 32, 34, 38, 40 and 44; FIG. 4 carries 22, 24, 36, 50, 52, 54, 56 and 58; FIG. 5 carries 18, 20, 70 and 80; FIG. 6 carries 10, 12, 18, 22, 24 and 28. That union is all 26 numerals in draft/numerals.md, and the twelve reported as absent, 18, 32, 36, 38, 44, 50, 52, 54, 56, 58, 70 and 80, are exactly the numerals that live only on the four unrendered sheets. So the coverage failure is a symptom of the missing sheets, and I removed no part, numeral definition, or supporting text to silence it. Every numeral listed on a sheet is also named in that sheet's prose, no sheet lists more than eight numerals, the Brief Description lists exactly the six figures the briefs describe, and the detailed description calls out each of FIG. 1 through FIG. 6. Section designation 3-3 remains identical in the FIG. 1 brief, the FIG. 3 brief, draft/07-drawings.md and draft/08-detailed-description.md. Each brief is within the character limit, the longest bodies being about 2668 for FIG. 4 and about 2653 for FIG. 6. To reduce the chance that a regeneration stalls or renders ambiguously, I made two small hardening edits in the affected briefs and nothing else. In FIG. 4, the sentence fixing the latch handle to the housing now states the contact positively, that its lower end meets the outer surface of the top wall of the latch housing 58 so the bar stands on the housing, the meeting drawn as a plain contact, instead of listing what is not depicted there; the same paragraph already marks the handle's attitude schematic and disclaims any particular angle or over-center geometry, so nothing is asserted that was not asserted before. In FIG. 3, the radial guide leader now targets a side wall of the channel holding the jaw carriage 30 rather than the right wall, since the earlier fix removed the statement placing the groove and channel on particular sides of that view and left the ordinal without a fixed referent. The remaining step is mechanical and belongs to the image pipeline: regenerate the four missing sheets from the existing briefs and re-run the numeral, leader, OCR and geometry checks. No claim, description, drawing description, Abstract or numeral-table text changed this turn.
reasoning: Before touching anything I checked whether the coverage failure indicated a real plan defect. It does not: the twelve missing numerals map exactly onto FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5, and the numerals shared with FIG. 1 or FIG. 2 were not reported. That pattern only occurs when those sheets exist as specifications but not as images, so redistributing labels or adding a sheet would have damaged a correct plan.

I deliberately did not move any numeral onto FIG. 1 or FIG. 2 to make the check pass. Those two views cannot show a sectioned guide, a follower in its slot, the latch drive train or the mounting boss, and forcing their numerals onto a plan view would have produced leaders pointing at nothing and broken the rule that each numeral denotes one part in every view.

The FIG. 4 handle sentence was worth rewording on its own terms. It had been phrased as a list of things not depicted, which is the kind of negative control that gives a renderer nothing positive to draw; stating the contact affirmatively keeps the handle attached, which was the point of the earlier fix, without relying on a prohibition.

The FIG. 3 leader fix repairs a loose end left by the previous pass. When the groove-and-channel side placement came out of that brief, the phrase the right wall lost its anchor, so the target now names a side wall generically, which still distinguishes the guide surface from the carriage body it holds.

I left the application text alone because the review raised nothing against it and my own pass found nothing: numerals are one-to-one, the section designation matches in all four required places, the Brief Description and the detailed description agree with the six briefs, and no placeholder or drafting note is present.

input.summary: The three reviewer findings are fixed in the briefs. FIG. 4 now shows the drive train unbroken: the zigzag line runs upward from the wedge 52 to the lower end of the latch handle 50, and the handle's lower end passes through an opening in the top wall of the latch housing 58 to meet the upper end of the force-limiting spring stack 54, so the bar is continuous with the drive train, with the form of that meeting shown schematically and asserting no pivot or mounting detail. That makes the sheet show what the Brief Description says it shows, the drive train between the latch handle and the segmented cam ring, and it matches the description's statement that the spring stack lies in a drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The naming inconsistency in FIG. 1 is gone: the element formerly called a lever is now described as a straight bar of the latch 16 reaching radially outward from the schematic latch block, its attitude shown schematically and drawn inclined toward the first frame half 10 to represent the latch in the over-center position, so no second name for the latch handle survives anywhere in the briefs. I did not add numeral 50 to the FIG. 1 list, because that sheet already carries eight numerals, which is the per-sheet ceiling, and numeral 50 already has its home on FIG. 4; describing the bar generically as part of the numbered latch 16 removes the competing name without overcrowding the sheet or touching any specification text. The generic-word collision is also gone: the annular guide 18 is a groove in FIG. 3, FIG. 5 and FIG. 6 alike, and channel now names only the radial guide 38 in FIG. 3, with the FIG. 6 numeral entries for 10, 12 and 18 updated to the same word. Adding the drive-train continuity took FIG. 4 past the character limit, so I trimmed the same brief where it had become repetitive: the meeting hedge no longer repeats the angle and over-center carve-out that the preceding sentence already makes, and the wedge sentence states that the direction of ring movement in that view is unspecified without also labelling it schematic. FIG. 4 now measures about 2744 characters, FIG. 1 about 2578 and FIG. 6 about 2642, all within the limit. The three mechanical checks remain rendering-stage: figures/ still holds only the six briefs, so FIG. 3 through FIG. 6 register as missing sheets, the FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 pixel consensus has no pixels to read, and the twelve listed numerals register as absent because they appear only on unrendered sheets. Sheet by sheet the briefs place all 26 numerals of draft/numerals.md, so no numeral was moved or removed and no application text changed this turn.
reasoning: The FIG. 4 defect was real and worth fixing exactly as identified: a sectioned, hatched wall drawn between the handle and the spring stack shows the handle outside the drive train, which is the one relationship the Brief Description promises that figure shows. The continuity is disclosed, since the inventor says the spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so drawing it costs nothing in fidelity.

On the FIG. 1 naming I fixed the defect the finding names, one element with two names, but not by adding a ninth numeral to that sheet. The eight-numeral ceiling exists so leaders stay readable, numeral 50 is already carried by FIG. 4, and the alternative of freeing a slot would have meant stripping a numeral such as the jaw pad from a sheet the detailed description ties it to. Describing the bar as part of the numbered latch 16 removes the second name outright.

The groove and channel collision was worth taking seriously because both words name real, separately numbered guides. Standardising on groove for the annular guide across the three briefs that show it, and reserving channel for the radial guide in the one brief that shows it, leaves no word mapping onto two parts.

The trims in FIG. 4 came out of the same paragraphs the additions went into, and only where the text had begun repeating its own hedges: the handle sentence already says the attitude is schematic and asserts no angle or over-center geometry, so the following clause did not need to say it again.

I again left the specification and the numeral assignments alone. The reviewer verified that the briefs place every specification numeral on a sheet and that the failures follow from sheets never having been rendered, so the corrective work here is confined to the briefs, and I created no image file since figure files in this workspace are Markdown specifications only.

The independent claims are unchanged and continue to rest on the relationship the inventor calls essential: closing the frame halves is itself what couples the two cam ring segments into one ring through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, a wedge moved by the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns that coupled ring through a stroke, three oblique slots convert the rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, and a force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. The Background states the technical problems that combination addresses before they are needed in argument: dividing the drive element with the body surrenders the fixed relationship between the two sides so the clamp settles off center, and a rigid handle drive train forces residual travel into whichever pad touched first while an instrument reading jaw position reports pipe size rather than grip force. tool_use_result.originalFile:
Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.

A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. If the gripping surfaces of each part are driven separately, the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive is given up: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. If the split body is instead pulled closed on the pipe, the closing force passes through the joint at the split and the pipe itself reacts the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe, and a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is needed, so that a different pipe size calls for a different part.

Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Concentrated loading of a single gripping surface is undesirable, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. An added instrument that responds to the position of the gripping elements reports the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.

What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.

content.content: 5	FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the split pipe clamp closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

The pipe 90 is seen end on at the centre of the drawing area as a circle with its interior blank. An annular frame body surrounds it, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from the pipe 90 and by an outer circle. The ring-shaped space between the pipe 90 and that inner circle is open, crossed only by the jaw pads 40 and the inner ends of the blocks that carry them.

Two radial joint lines, at the left and at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10, the lower the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, shown schematically as a small circle on that joint line between the inner circle and the outer circle.

At the right joint is the latch 16, shown schematically as a rectangular block outside the frame body bridging both frame ends, with the latch handle 50 reaching radially outward from that block as a straight bar, the handle's attitude shown schematically, drawn inclined toward the first frame half 10 to represent the latch in the over-center position.

Three blocks are spaced around the annular frame body, at the top, the lower left and the lower right, one on the first frame half 10 and two on the second frame half 12, these three circumferential positions and their distribution between the two frame halves being shown schematically. At each position the inner circle is interrupted by a radial opening and the block is shown schematically as reaching radially inward through that opening, its outer portion within the body and its inner end inside the inner circle.

Each block carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies in the upper part of the view on the radial centre line of the topmost block, its outer end just outside the outer circle and its inner end at the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points horizontally to the right, both on the same side of the line, giving the direction in which FIG. 3 is viewed. Each end carries the numeral 3 as the section designation, just outside that end beside its arrow, so the line reads as line 3-3; it is a section designation rather than a reference numeral, and no leader line runs to it.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer circle of the frame body at the upper left, away from the pipe 90.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the inner end of the topmost block.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar reaching radially outward from the latch block.
- 90 pipe: target the interior of the central circle, inside the inner circle.

input.summary: Both findings are fixed. In figures/FIG-1.md the element at the right joint is now the latch handle 50, reaching radially outward from the schematic latch block as a straight bar, with the handle's attitude shown schematically and drawn inclined toward the first frame half 10 to represent the latch in the over-center position, and numeral 50 was added to that sheet's list with a target well inside the straight bar reaching radially outward from the latch block. The element now carries one name and one numeral everywhere it appears, matching draft/numerals.md, the detailed description and the FIG. 4 brief. Adding 50 would have made nine numerals on that sheet, above the eight-per-sheet ceiling, so I moved jaw carriage 30 to the focused view that already carries it, FIG. 3, which is the sectional view of one jaw carriage with its follower, radial guide and return spring. Following the numeral-moving procedure, every use of that numeral and its canonical part name is gone from the FIG. 1 brief: the three carriages are now described there as three blocks spaced around the annular frame body, one on the first frame half 10 and two on the second frame half 12, each reaching radially inward through an opening in the inner circle, and the cutting-plane line now lies on the radial centre line of the topmost block. That required no change to the specification, because the detailed description ties FIG. 1 to the clamp 100, the pipe 90, the jaw pads 40, the two halves, the hinge 14 and the latch 16, and discusses the jaw carriages 30 without saying they are shown in FIG. 1, while expressly referring the carriage detail to FIG. 3. FIG. 1 now lists 100, 10, 12, 14, 16, 40, 50 and 90, which is eight, and the six sheets together still place all 26 numerals: 30 is carried by FIG. 3, and nothing was deleted or left without a home. In draft/05-background.md the closing paragraph now reads that it would be desirable to provide a split clamp in which the drive is coupled by the act of closing, every gripping element is advanced from that one drive, and the remaining lever travel is absorbed within the clamp and reported as a loading condition rather than a dimension, replacing the assertion about what has been lacking. The need is stated in the same terms without a factual claim about the field that no reference in prior_art/ supports. The three mechanical checks remain rendering-stage: figures/ still holds only the six briefs, so FIG. 3 through FIG. 6 register as missing sheets, the FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 semantic consensus has no pixels to read, and the twelve listed numerals register as absent because they appear only on unrendered sheets. All briefs stay within the character limit, the largest being FIG. 6 at about 2642 characters and FIG. 4 at about 2744.
reasoning: The naming defect was real and had survived a previous pass in a different form, so I gave the element its canonical name and numeral rather than reaching for another generic word. Calling it the latch handle 50 in FIG. 1 costs nothing in fidelity, since the handle is disclosed and the brief still marks its attitude as schematic.

That fix collided with the eight-numeral ceiling, and I resolved the collision by moving a numeral out rather than by crowding the sheet or inventing a seventh figure. Jaw carriage 30 was the right one to move: FIG. 3 is the focused sectional view of exactly that part and already carries it, so coverage is untouched.

I checked the description before moving it, because moving a numeral off a sheet is only safe if no text says that part is visible there. The FIG. 1 paragraph names the clamp, the pipe, the pads, the halves, the hinge and the latch, and the carriage paragraph carries no figure reference and already points the carriage detail to FIG. 3, so no specification sentence had to be edited to keep text and figures in step.

Having removed the numeral, I removed the canonical name with it and described the carriages as plain blocks, which is what the procedure requires when a sheet still needs the structure only as context. The pads remain numbered on FIG. 1 because the description says they are seated on the pipe in that view.

On the Background, the substance of the paragraph is the need the invention answers, not a survey of what exists, so restating it as a desideratum keeps the entire technical argument intact while removing the one sentence that asserted a fact about the field with no reference behind it. The earlier paragraphs already read as mechanical reasoning about split clamps rather than as claims about identified art.

With no art of record, the Background now states the problems and the need in its own terms rather than asserting what the field lacks: dividing the drive element with the body surrenders the fixed relationship between the two sides so the clamp settles off center, a split body pulled closed on the pipe needs a part dimensioned to a particular diameter, and a rigid handle drive train forces residual travel into whichever pad touched first while an instrument reading jaw position reports pipe size rather than grip force. The independent claims are unchanged and continue to rest on the relationship the inventor calls essential: closing the frame halves is itself what couples the two cam ring segments into one ring through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, a wedge moved by the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns that coupled ring through a stroke, three oblique slots convert the rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, and a force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. That explanation sits in the specification ahead of any argument that may need it. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art available here may be incomplete and a later search could surface references bearing on these claims.
